The audio signal processing unit (34) comprises: a beamformer unit (24) configured to process the captured audio signals to generate the output audio signal in a manner that creates an acoustic beam having a direction; a direction-of-arrival, DOA, unit (30) configured to determine the direction of arrival of sound by analyzing the captured audio signals; and a control unit (26) configured to control the beamformer unit. A clip-mounted microphone assembly is described. The assembly includes a fastening mechanism (16) that allows the microphone assembly (10) to be secured to a user’s clothing (11). It also includes at least three microphones (20, 21, 22) that receive audio signals from the user’s voice and together establish a microphone plane.

The assembly further comprises an acceleration sensor (32) configured to detect gravitational acceleration in at least two perpendicular directions and, based on that detection, generate an orientation signal. An audio signal processing unit (34) produces an output audio signal (36) from the audio signals captured by the microphones. This processing unit includes a beamformer unit (24), which processes the captured signals to form an acoustic beam having a particular direction, thereby generating the output audio signal.

In addition, the assembly includes a direction-of-arrival unit (30) that identifies the arrival direction of sound by evaluating the captured audio signals. A control unit (26) controls the beamformer unit and is configured to determine a permitted angular range (40) for the acoustic beam direction using the orientation signal. The control unit then directs the acoustic beam within that permitted angular range according to the determined direction of arrival.

The clip-on microphone assembly is designed to be worn by a user and attached to the user’s clothing by means of a clip-on mechanism. The clip-on mechanism allows the assembly to be removably secured to garments such as a shirt, jacket, collar, lapel, or other suitable item of clothing, positioning the microphones close to the user’s mouth during use.

The assembly includes at least three microphones arranged to capture the user’s voice. The microphones are positioned relative to one another so that they define a microphone plane. By using three or more microphones, the assembly is able to obtain spatial audio information that can be used to distinguish the user’s speech from surrounding noise and to determine the direction from which sound is arriving.

The assembly further includes an acceleration sensor configured to sense gravitational acceleration in at least two orthogonal dimensions. Based on the sensed gravitational acceleration, the acceleration sensor generates an orientation signal that indicates the orientation of the microphone assembly when it is worn by the user. This orientation signal may be used to determine how the microphone plane is positioned relative to gravity and, therefore, relative to the expected location of the user’s mouth.

An audio signal processing unit receives audio signals from the microphones and processes those signals using beamforming and direction-of-arrival analysis. The direction-of-arrival analysis identifies a detected direction from which sound, such as the user’s voice, is received. The beamforming process then combines the microphone signals in a manner that emphasizes sound from a selected direction while reducing sound from other directions, thereby producing an improved output audio signal.

A control unit is operatively connected to the acceleration sensor and the audio signal processing unit. The control unit determines an allowed angular sector based on the orientation signal. This allowed angular sector defines a range of directions in which the user’s mouth is expected to be located, taking into account the current orientation of the clip-on microphone assembly. The control unit then controls the audio signal processing unit so that the acoustic beam is steered within the allowed angular sector according to the detected direction of arrival of the sound. In this way, the assembly can adapt to different wearing positions while maintaining directional focus on the user’s voice and reducing interference from unwanted sounds outside the allowed sector.
outputs.L4:
A clip-on microphone assembly is designed to improve the capture of a user’s voice in environments where background noise, clothing noise, and changing microphone orientation can degrade audio quality. The assembly includes a compact housing that can be attached to a user’s clothing, such as a collar, lapel, shirt, jacket, or lanyard. Within or on the housing are at least three microphones arranged at known positions relative to one another. The microphones generate multiple audio signals from the surrounding sound field, allowing the system to compare differences in timing, phase, and level between the signals. These differences are used to estimate the direction from which speech and other sounds arrive.

The assembly also includes an acceleration sensor, such as an accelerometer or inertial sensor, that detects the physical orientation and movement of the device. Because a clip-on microphone may be worn at different angles depending on clothing, body posture, or how it is attached, the direction of the user’s mouth relative to the microphone array may vary significantly. The acceleration sensor provides orientation information that helps the signal processor determine how the microphone assembly is positioned during use. This orientation information can be used to identify an expected angular region in which the user’s voice is likely to be located.

A signal processing unit receives the audio signals from the microphones and the orientation data from the acceleration sensor. The processor performs direction-of-arrival analysis to estimate where dominant sound sources are located relative to the microphone array. Using the known microphone geometry, the processor analyzes the received signals and determines whether detected sound energy is likely to correspond to the user’s speech or to unwanted noise from another direction. The system may continuously or periodically update this estimate as the user moves, turns, or changes posture.

Based on the direction-of-arrival information, the processor forms an acoustic beam that is steered toward the user’s mouth or toward the most likely direction of the desired voice signal. Beamforming techniques combine the microphone signals in a way that reinforces sound arriving from the selected direction while reducing sound arriving from other directions. This improves the clarity and level of the user’s voice and reduces interference from nearby talkers, ambient noise, machinery, wind, or reverberation.

A key feature of the assembly is that beam steering is made orientation-aware. Rather than allowing the beamformer to steer freely toward any detected sound source, the system restricts beam steering to an allowed angular sector. This allowed sector is determined at least in part from the orientation of the clip-on device, as measured by the acceleration sensor. For example, if the device is clipped to the user’s chest or collar, the system can define a sector that corresponds to the expected direction of the user’s mouth. Sounds arriving from outside this sector may be treated as less likely to be the desired voice and may be suppressed or ignored for beam-steering purposes.

By limiting beam steering to a permitted angular range, the microphone assembly reduces the risk of accidentally steering toward an undesired sound source, such as another person speaking nearby or a loud noise in the environment. This is particularly useful for wearable microphones because the device may rotate, tilt, or shift during normal use. The acceleration sensor enables the processor to compensate for these changes and maintain an appropriate relationship between the device orientation and the expected speech direction.

The result is a wearable microphone system that provides more reliable voice pickup than a conventional single microphone or a beamformer that does not account for orientation. The use of at least three microphones supports robust spatial analysis, while the acceleration sensor provides contextual information about how the device is being worn. Together, these components allow the signal processor to form and steer an acoustic beam within a controlled angular sector, improving speech intelligibility and reducing unwanted sound from outside the intended pickup region.

However, being labeled DOA does not always mean the end. There can still be lessons hidden in failed attempts. counterfactuals.output: A clip-on microphone assembly includes a housing configured to attach to a user’s clothing, three spatially separated microphones supported by the housing, and an inertial sensor, such as an accelerometer, configured to determine an orientation of the housing. Processing circuitry receives audio signals from the microphones and orientation data from the inertial sensor, estimates a direction of arrival of acoustic energy using the audio signals, and defines an allowed angular sector based at least in part on the determined orientation. The processing circuitry selects or constrains the estimated direction of arrival to the allowed angular sector and applies beamforming to the audio signals using the constrained direction of arrival to generate an enhanced audio output. By limiting beamforming steering to an orientation-dependent angular sector, the assembly may reduce capture of undesired sound sources and improve pickup of speech from an intended talker despite variable attachment orientation of the clip-on assembly.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a technical description of a lavalier microphone system that uses multiple microphones and an accelerometer to determine orientation and restrict beamforming direction based on direction-of-arrival analysis.
counterfactuals.output:
A lavalier microphone system includes a compact microphone assembly configured to be worn on a user’s clothing and to capture speech while reducing off-axis noise. The assembly incorporates a plurality of spatially separated microphone elements, an inertial sensor such as a three-axis accelerometer, and a signal-processing circuit configured to perform direction-of-arrival estimation and adaptive beamforming.

The microphone elements may be arranged in a small array within the lavalier housing, for example as two or more omnidirectional MEMS microphones positioned at known relative locations. Each microphone produces a corresponding audio signal. Because sound from a given acoustic source reaches each microphone at slightly different times and phases, the system can estimate a direction of arrival of the acoustic energy by comparing inter-microphone time differences, phase differences, coherence, or other spatial features.

The accelerometer provides an indication of the physical orientation of the lavalier assembly relative to gravity. Since a lavalier microphone may be clipped to clothing in different orientations, twisted, tilted, or inverted during use, the accelerometer data is used to determine the current orientation of the microphone array. The processor maps the microphone-array coordinate system to an external reference frame or to an expected wearer-relative frame based on the accelerometer output.

Using the orientation information, the system defines one or more permissible beamforming regions. For example, the processor may identify a forward/upward region corresponding to the expected location of the wearer’s mouth and exclude directions corresponding to the wearer’s chest, the floor, or surrounding noise sources. The permissible region may be expressed as an angular sector, cone, or set of allowable azimuth/elevation ranges relative to the measured orientation of the microphone housing.

The processor then performs direction-of-arrival analysis on incoming audio. If the estimated direction of arrival falls within the permitted region, the system may steer or maintain a beamformer in that direction. If the estimated direction falls outside the permitted region, the system may inhibit beam steering toward that direction, attenuate the corresponding signal component, reject the direction-of-arrival estimate, or constrain the beamformer to the nearest allowed direction.

In one implementation, the system operates as follows:

1. The microphones acquire multiple audio channels.
2. The accelerometer measures the orientation of the lavalier housing.
3. The processor determines the array orientation and calculates an allowed acoustic capture region relative to the user.
4. Direction-of-arrival estimation is performed using the microphone signals.
5. The estimated source direction is compared with the allowed region.
6. A beamformer is steered only toward directions that satisfy the orientation-based constraint.
7. Signals arriving from disallowed directions are suppressed or prevented from influencing the beamforming solution.

The beamformer may use delay-and-sum processing, minimum-variance distortionless response processing, generalized sidelobe cancellation, adaptive noise cancellation, or another spatial filtering technique. The orientation constraint reduces the likelihood that the beamformer will lock onto an undesired acoustic source, such as environmental noise, a nearby talker, clothing rustle, or reflections from surfaces.

The accelerometer may also be used to detect gross changes in mounting position. When the lavalier is rotated or inverted, the system updates the mapping between microphone-array coordinates and the expected mouth direction. This allows the microphone to provide consistent directional pickup even when clipped at different angles.

The system may further include calibration data describing the geometry of the microphone array, accelerometer alignment, and preferred pickup direction. In some embodiments, a confidence measure may be assigned to each direction-of-arrival estimate. Beam steering may occur only when both the direction estimate confidence exceeds a threshold and the estimated direction lies within the accelerometer-derived allowable region.

This arrangement enables a wearable lavalier microphone to combine spatial audio capture with orientation awareness. By restricting beamforming based on direction-of-arrival analysis and measured device orientation, the system improves speech pickup from the wearer while reducing sensitivity to sounds arriving from unintended directions.
